vectors.description: The smallest complete document there is: envelope version 1, a registered kind, and the smallest body. Every other envelope vector differs from this one in exactly one member.

An envelope at a version this specification does not define. A v1 reader refuses it whole and names both versions — reading it partially would let a member it has no field for satisfy a requirement by omission.
A body shape that is not in the kind registry. Refused with `unknownDocumentKind`, never guessed at from the body's shape — the refusal is how a reader discovers it is older than its counterparty.
An envelope with no body at all. Well-formed JSON, not a well-formed envelope.
A vintage pinned all the way down to the bytes: dataset, version, format, content address and row count. The row count is the corpus's first sign-prefixed 64-bit integer.
The ordinary submitter shape: which vintage, with the content ref left for the executor to resolve. A null content ref is conformant, not incomplete.
The executor's answer to 'what is this, exactly?' — the ref with its content ref present, when it came into existence, and whether it was the latest at the moment of asking.
A format identifier with an uppercase letter and a space. An UNREGISTERED format is not an error — the registry is open — but an identifier that can never be registered is always a defect.
One fit: an opaque payload with the hash its submitter minted, a provider kind, a seed, three gates authored out of order and emitted sorted, and the submitter class.

Three submissions under one correlation id, one per submitter class, in the SUBMITTER's order — the one list in this specification that is not sorted, because the receipt indexes into it. Carries a negative seed and a seed beyond exact double range.
Partial acceptance as data: two items enqueued with job handles, one refused with a typed refusal carrying the providers that WERE available. The two lists partition the submitted indices exactly.
A batch with no submissions. A receipt for nothing is indistinguishable from a receipt whose items were all lost.
A gate direction outside the closed vocabulary. Refused rather than defaulted: a gate whose direction is guessed is a gate that silently passes.
A submitter class outside the closed vocabulary. Defaulting an unknown class to `human` would make the stricter policy path unreachable by exactly the callers it exists for.
An empty spec hash. The executor cannot mint one — the payload is opaque to it — so a submission with no hash is a fit that can never be joined to the decision that asked for it.

Gates that state the unit of their threshold (§5.3) — kilograms, the dimensionless `1` — beside one that states none, which omits the member rather than writing `null` (§3.1 rule 5). Authored out of order and emitted sorted.
A gate whose unit is not unit text (§3.5). Refused before anything is scheduled: a threshold in a unit nobody can read is a threshold nobody can compare against.

The join, on its own. `digest` is the content address over the canonical bytes of the BODY — the value every implementation must reproduce, and the one number in this corpus that two parties sharing no type must independently agree on.

A fit that ran, passed its gates and was approved. Diagnostics and verdicts authored out of order and emitted sorted; a non-finite diagnostic dropped rather than encoded; `digest` recomputed over the embedded composite key, and equal to the document's own `compositeKeyHash`.
A fit that ran, failed both gates, retained no artifact, and was registered anyway — a failure is evidence. Also the corpus's empty-map and null-cost case.

An outcome whose stated identity does not match a recomputation over its own composite key. Corrupt or edited after registration — refused, never stored. Schema-valid by construction: only the identity rule catches it.

A backend that states what its diagnostics measure (§5.4): an error in kilograms, a dimensionless ratio, a mean absolute error in pence, and one diagnostic stated with no unit. A non-finite diagnostic is dropped and its unit with it; gate verdicts carry the unit of their threshold, the verdict on the unit-less diagnostic none.
A diagnostic unit that does not parse (§3.5): a space where the grammar wants `.` or `/`. Schema-valid by construction — a unit is a string to a schema — so only the unit-text rule catches it.
A unit that parses but is not its canonical text (§3.5): `s-1` where the unit is written `/s`. Refused rather than normalised — two texts for one unit would give one outcome two encodings.
A unit for a diagnostic the outcome does not carry (§5.4). A statement about nothing, and the one shape in which a reader could not tell a lost diagnostic from an invented unit.

A verdict whose threshold is in grams over an error reported in kilograms (§5.3's gate rule). The comparison it records is one no executor may make, so an outcome carrying it is refused, never stored.
A conjunctive multi-key query with every filter list authored out of order and emitted sorted, and a first page (null cursor).
The match-anything query — every filter empty — resuming from an opaque cursor at the maximum page size. Empty is 'any', never 'nothing'.
A page of two outcomes ordered by composite-key hash — a value that exists before an outcome is stored and never changes, which is what makes paging stable while new outcomes are being registered.
The last page: a null cursor is the terminator, and is the only thing that ends a paging loop.
A page size of zero. Answering it with a default page size would make a caller's loop silently ask for something else than it asked for.
The last page, holding an outcome that states no units beside one that states them: the units travel with the outcome, and the outcome without them keeps the bytes it has in every other vector.
Apply a registered artifact — named by the composite-key hash of the outcome that produced it — to an input vintage, with predictions landing in a distinct dataset.
Predictions asked to land as a new version of the very dataset they were derived from. Schema-valid; caught only by comparing the two identifiers.
The refusal a version-unsupported envelope produces, naming both what arrived and what is accepted.
An unimplemented body shape, with the kinds this participant does implement — so the caller re-aims without a second round trip.
A submission denied before any work was scheduled.
A malformed query — an out-of-range limit, an unknown status, an unusable cursor.
No provider of the requested kind here, with the kinds that ARE available, sorted.
Refused on cost grounds before it ran, with quota, spend and the accounting unit — the numbers a caller needs to decide whether to wait or to ask for less.
Work completed but did not clear its gates, and the executor's policy is to refuse rather than register. Carries the verdicts, so the submitter need not re-query to learn which gate.
A named policy refused it. The rule's identifier is stable; its wording is not.
The corpus's payload-free refusal: a class with no members is still an object with a `class`, never a bare string.
The scope resolved, and does not permit the operation. Distinct from having no scope at all.
No such thing in the caller's scope — deliberately indistinguishable from 'exists, but not yours'.
The capability is not composed in this deployment. Distinct from `notFound`: the thing asked for is not merely absent, it is not offered.
Scoring refused with a typed sub-reason from the score-reason registry, plus free-form detail that is diagnostic and not contractual.
The underlying store failed. The wording is not stable and must not be matched on; the class is.
The catch-all, so that nothing ever escapes as an exception. A refusal a program cannot branch on is still infinitely better than one it cannot detect.

A gate stated in grams against a diagnostic the provider reports in kilograms (§5.3's gate rule): refused by name, never converted. Registered after version 1, so every member is declared from its first day and `null` would stand where a side states no unit.

A refusal class registered after this version, carrying members a v1 reader has no field for. A conformant reader MUST accept it, read it as `unspecified`, keep whatever human-readable text it can find, and report the unrecognised class name. An implementation that refuses this vector is one that will break on the next additive change.

A rendering that is already in canonical form, so the rule's intermediate equals its input. The minting rule is a NORMALISATION, and this is its fixed point — the vector to start an implementation against, because a divergence here is a divergence in escaping or number formatting alone, with ordering not yet in play.

The same specification as `canonical-form`, authored with its members permuted at every level and indented across lines. Its own `sha256` differs; its `canonicalPayload` and `digest` are identical. That is §4.2 rule 3 made observable, and an implementation that reproduces every other vector but not this pairing has a canonicalisation that depends on authoring order. The term list is deliberately NOT permuted: an array's order is data, so permuting it would be a different specification rather than a different rendering of this one.

Number normalisation: negative zero becomes `0`, an exponent becomes its shortest round-trip decimal, a trailing zero is dropped, and a value small enough to keep its exponent keeps it. `identifier` carries a value beyond exact double range as a STRING — the shape §4.5 requires of a submitter, for the same reason §3.2 divergence 2 requires it on the wire.

Escaping and ordering over the whole character range: a quote, a backslash, a control character with a short escape, literal non-ASCII, and an astral-plane character. Two of the keys are non-ASCII and pin the ordering rule — keys sort by UTF-16 CODE UNIT (§3.1 rule 12), so the astral key sorts BEFORE U+FFFD; an implementation sorting by code point puts it after and mints a different hash for the same specification.

Structure: an empty object, an empty array, a null, a boolean, and an array of objects. The array keeps its order while each element's members sort — the two rules of §4.5 step 2 acting on the same value, which is where an implementation that sorts everything or sorts nothing shows itself.

`permuted-form` with its hash minted over the payload AS RENDERED instead of over the canonical bytes — the one implementation error the rule exists to exclude, and the only reject vector in this corpus a submitter rather than an executor must catch (§2). Nothing downstream is permitted to notice it (§4.2 rule 2): the executor stores it, keys by it, and every join against the submitter's own record silently misses. Schema-valid by construction — it is a well-formed content address over the wrong bytes.
